role.altitude: The bindery worker keeps reading jobs, checking sheets, watching machines, judging adjustments and coaching new colleagues; hunting for job bags, filling daily paper forms and checking every sample by eye shrink.
skills_to_grow: Using the job terminal and stop reasons
role.ambitious_version: A bindery worker whose counts and times record themselves, so the shift is spent at the machine.

tasks.short: Find the job ticket, read work orders to determine instructions and specifications for machine set-up, check them against the delivered sheets and clarify unclear points.

steps.what: Bindery worker finds the job bag and work order
Bindery worker reads work orders to determine instructions and specifications for machine set-up
Bindery worker checks the specifications against the delivered printed sheets
Bindery worker clarifies unclear points with planning or customer service

tasks.design: The job ticket from the print management system appears on a terminal at the bindery machine in planned order, with the current specification, instead of a paper job bag. Reading the specification, checking it against the sheets and asking questions stay with the bindery worker.
tasks.previous_blocker: Paper job bags travelled with the work and could be out of date.
tasks.enabler_now: Print management systems that send job tickets to the shop floor.
tasks.still_hard: Jobs whose sheets differ from the ticket.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing that a fold will not work on this paper.

reach.learn: Whether changes reach the machine in time.

evidence.claim: A print management system handles quotations, order forms, stock and cost price.

assumptions: Boundary: understanding the job before set-up; setting up is outside.
Input contract for s1: planning keeps job tickets current in the print management system.
Reading, checking and clarifying keep their full time; s1 keeps 50 for opening the job on the terminal and for jobs whose ticket is not yet current.
unknowns: Whether terminals exist in the bindery.
research_questions: Do jobs bound to an outdated specification stop?

incremental.description: Bindery worker reports wrong job tickets on the terminal.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: planning keeps only half of the tickets current, so the paper bag is still fetched for those jobs (3.5); high: tickets kept current as assumed (7.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Monitor machine operations to detect malfunctions, check sample products, determine whether adjustments are needed and note malfunctions.

steps.what: Bindery worker monitors machine operations to detect malfunctions
Bindery worker checks sample products for signature order and finish
Bindery worker determines whether adjustments are needed
Bindery worker notes malfunctions: in the paper machine log today, on the terminal after the change

tasks.design: On binding lines with signature recognition, the machine reads a code on each signature and stops on a wrong or missing one, so the bindery worker checks fewer samples by hand for order. Watching the machine and deciding adjustments stay with the worker. Malfunctions are still noted by the worker, on the terminal instead of a paper log.
tasks.previous_blocker: Signature order was checked by pulling samples.
tasks.enabler_now: Signature recognition on binding lines and stop-reason terminals.
tasks.still_hard: Faults like glue or trim quality that sensors miss.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing a machine sound wrong before it jams.

reach.learn: Whether stop reasons point to recurring faults.

evidence.claim: Signature recognition on binding lines can stop the machine on a wrong signature.

assumptions: Boundary: watching the machine during runs; repairs are outside.
Input contract for s2: signature codes printed by the press room on lines with recognition, about 60% of binding work; s2 is priced at that share.
Watching, deciding and noting malfunctions keep their full time; the note is a first record. s2 keeps 70 because order checks drop on lines with recognition while finish checks stay.
unknowns: Share of lines with signature recognition.

incremental.description: Bindery worker checks the recognition camera at start-up.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the press room prints codes for only half of the work planned, so most sample checks stay (2.7); high: about 60% of work on lines with recognition (5.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Record counts of finished products, job times and stops, materials and waste, complete the daily production records form and check the day's record.

steps.what: Bindery worker records counts of finished products

Bindery worker records job start and stop times and machine stops: on the paper form today; after the change by scanning the job ticket at start and stop, with stops on connected machines logged by the machine and the worker entering each stop reason
Bindery worker records materials used and waste: on the paper form today; after the change the job's materials are listed from the ticket and the worker enters the quantities used and wasted
Bindery worker completes the daily production records form and hands it in
Bindery worker checks the day's record: counts, times, stops, materials and waste against the day's jobs
Bindery worker confirms the checked day's record to the shift leader

tasks.design: Connected machines send their counters to the shop-floor records, and hand work is counted and entered on the terminal. The bindery worker scans the job ticket to start and stop a job, picks stop reasons and enters the quantities of materials and waste against the job's material list. The daily form is built from these entries, so the paper form vanishes; the worker checks the day's record and confirms it once to the shift leader. Records are per machine and job; any use to rate individuals needs works council consent first.

approvals.approved_version: The day's production record with counts, times, stops, materials and waste exactly as checked by the bindery worker in s5, confirmed once to the shift leader in the shop-floor records; any change needs a new check and confirmation.

tasks.previous_blocker: Daily paper forms were filled by hand and typed in the office.
tasks.enabler_now: Machine counters and shop-floor terminals linked to the print management system.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing a count is wrong because the pallet looks short.
tasks.altitude: Much less form filling; checking stays.

reach.learn: Whether output figures are available during the shift.

evidence.claim: A print management system handles order forms, stock and cost price; its vendor projects admin hours saved, a projection not a measurement.
Data that logs output per operator or shift can check performance and needs works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: daily production records in the bindery; costing is outside.
Input contract for s1: machine counters on connected machines, about 70% of output; the rest counted by hand and entered on the terminal; s1 is priced at that share.
Input contract for s4: the entries made in s1 to s3 on the terminal.

Checking and confirming keep their full time. s2 keeps 80 because scanning start and stop is the worker's own record, like writing the time, and only writing the stops of connected machines goes; s3 keeps 75 because quantities are still entered by the worker; s4 is gone because the form is built from the entries.
unknowns: Share of output on connected machines.
research_questions: Do job cost figures become more accurate?

incremental.description: Bindery worker corrects wrong machine counts on the terminal.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: half of the output is hand work with no counter and stops are not linked, so more is entered by hand (34.7); high: about 70% of output on connected machines as assumed (47.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Prepare training checklists and settings sheets, train workers at the machine to set up and operate automatic bindery machines, judge when they can run it alone and record the training.

steps.what: Bindery worker prepares training checklists and settings sheets
Bindery worker trains workers at the machine to set up and operate automatic bindery machines
Bindery worker judges when the trainee can run the machine alone
Bindery worker records the training done: on paper today, in the training register after the change

tasks.design: A standard training checklist and settings sheet per machine, written once and kept current, replaces preparing notes for each trainee. Training at the machine and judging readiness stay hands-on. The sign-off goes into the training register.
tasks.previous_blocker: Training notes were prepared fresh for each trainee.
tasks.enabler_now: Shared checklists and simple training registers.
tasks.human_edge: Showing how a setting feels when it is right.

evidence.claim: Standard checklists and registers replace notes prepared per trainee.

assumptions: Boundary: training on bindery machines; hiring is outside.

Training, sign-off and recording the training keep their full time; the record is a first write. s1 keeps 70 because the standard checklist replaces fresh notes and the worker still adapts it to each trainee.
research_questions: Do new workers make fewer set-up errors?

incremental.description: Bindery worker updates checklists when machines change.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: one trainee a year, so the standard checklist is rarely reused (1.7); high: several trainees on several machines (5.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
